expectations.text: The reply opens with the recommendation and does not put the whole product and engineering organisation on the rebrand: it protects capacity for the top customer problems.
expectations.evidence: 'My recommendation is to split Q1 into two protected tracks, put a hard cap on the rebrand, and bring leadership a trade-off with numbers instead of a refusal.'

expectations.text: The reply splits the rebrand into a small must-have part (for example the name in the app, domain redirects, legal text) and parts that can wait or be phased (for example a full design system), and makes the cost of each visible.
expectations.evidence: 'Break it into the four items: name in the app, design system, new domain, marketing site. Estimate engineering and design weeks for each... the design system is the largest and least time-bound item, and the domain move carries the most hidden risk'; 'What to defer to Q2: the full design system rollout... Ship the new name, logo, colours and typography through tokens and a thin theme layer now'.

expectations.text: The reply ranks the customer problems with evidence (for example NPS comments, churn or revenue at risk, support tickets) and sets measures for fixing them.
expectations.evidence: It asks 'Which accounts mention invoicing, the accounting integration or reports in NPS verbatims, support tickets and churn or cancellation notes? Convert to ARR at risk', but rolls the answer into one figure ('€X of ARR sits with accounts that named these three issues'). Per-fix measures are good (p95 invoice time, integration error rate, report usage), but the three problems are never ranked against each other; only 'the highest-value missing reports' are.

expectations.text: The reply brings leadership options with explicit trade-offs instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: It brings one proposal (the two-track split, with a CEO script) and treats the all-in rebrand only as a fallback ('If the CEO insists on 100% rebrand...'). The cost of the status quo is stated ('we are choosing to leave invoicing broken for another quarter'), but there is no set of options for leadership to choose from.

expectations.text: The reply handles "leadership decides, teams execute" and "any decision beats no decision" constructively: a private conversation first, asking for the reasons, separating decisions that are cheap to reverse from ones that aren't, and offering a light decision process, without labelling or attacking the leaders.
expectations.evidence: Constructive in tone ('don't go in saying "the rebrand is wrong"'), with a checkpoint ('if the customer metrics are not moving by week 6, we re-decide together') and a written decision if overruled. But there's no private conversation first, no asking leadership for its reasons, and no split of the slogans into cheap-to-reverse and costly decisions ('safe and reversible' is only used to sequence the work).

expectations.text: The reply is practical and short enough to act on (roughly 500 words or less), with any longer plan offered or attached as a separate document.
expectations.evidence: reply.md is 1,252 words (wc -w), far above the 550 ceiling, and no separate document was attached.

factual_errors.evidence: The domain-migration risks (SEO, email deliverability, SSO and OAuth redirect URIs, allowlists, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, webhooks) are accurate. No wrong claims found.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: No leader says the responsibility for the NPS fall or the open complaints is leadership's.

best_insight.value: 'Never change the thing customers rely on (invoicing, integration) in the same window as the thing that touches how they reach you (domain, SSO, email). One risky change at a time.'

suggestions.assertion: The reply ranks the customer problems with evidence (for example NPS comments, churn or revenue at risk, support tickets) and sets measures for fixing them.
suggestions.reason: 'Ranks' is ambiguous. Most replies ask for evidence on the three complaints together and set measures, but few put them in order. I passed a sample only when it broke the evidence down per complaint (ARR, tickets or detractor comments per issue) or gave an explicit order. Consider rewording to 'sizes each complaint with its own evidence and puts them in order'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply handles "leadership decides, teams execute" and "any decision beats no decision" constructively: a private conversation first, asking for the reasons, separating decisions that are cheap to reverse from ones that aren't, and offering a light decision process, without labelling or attacking the leaders.
suggestions.reason: This assertion bundles four required behaviours plus a tone check. Several strong samples met three of the four and failed on one (usually asking for the reasons, or splitting reversible from irreversible decisions). Splitting it into two assertions would give a clearer signal.

No assertion checks the technical link between the new domain and the broken accounting integration (OAuth redirect URIs, webhooks, sending-domain reputation, customer allowlists). Most samples raised it, and it is the most practical sequencing argument. Capacity realism (no overtime, slack for incidents) and committing to the decision once it is made also go unchecked.

eval_feedback.overall: Detailed delivery plan with good risk sequencing, but far too long, it offers one plan rather than options, and it doesn't handle the CEO's slogans with a private conversation or questions.
